title: `Map`, `Set`, `WeakMap`, `Symbol`
summary: Collections that keep keys and values by identity, and symbols as property keys that never collide.

misconceptions.description: Believes a Map turns its keys into text, so 7 and "7", or any two objects, become the same key.
Believes Map lookups match keys loosely, so get(7) can find the entry stored under "7".
Believes a Map compares object keys by their contents instead of by identity.
Believes map[key] = value stores a Map entry the way it stores an object property.
Believes a Set holds every value added to it, repeats included.
Believes a value added twice is removed from a Set entirely instead of kept once.
Believes a Set compares values with ===, so NaN is never a repeat.
Believes a WeakMap accepts keys of any type, like a Map.
Believes WeakMap entries disappear as soon as they are set, or are already gone when observed.
Believes a WeakMap can be sized or counted, for example through a size method.
Believes two symbols with the same description are the same symbol.
Believes a symbol prints as its bare description text.
Believes a symbol-keyed property cannot be read by code that holds the symbol.

lessons.title: Map keeps keys as they are

conceptCard.title: A Map keeps every key as it is
conceptCard.body: A Map stores key and value pairs. A key can be any value, and it keeps its type: 1 and "1" are different keys. Objects are compared by identity. The set method adds an entry, get reads one, size counts them, and a loop gives entries in insertion order.

conceptCard.title: A Set keeps each value once
conceptCard.body: A Set is a collection with no repeated values. add ignores a value that is already inside, has tests for it, and size counts the values. A Set is iterable in insertion order, so spreading it gives an array without repeats.

conceptCard.title: Weak collections need object keys
conceptCard.body: WeakMap keys and WeakSet values must be objects (non-registered symbols are allowed too). They cannot be counted or looped over, and have no size. You use them only with an object you already hold: get, set, has, delete and add. Their entries do not keep an object alive.

conceptCard.title: Every symbol is unique
conceptCard.body: Symbol(text) returns a new unique value; the text is only a description. Symbols can be property keys, written as [sym], and are skipped by Object.keys and for...in. Symbol.for(text) returns one shared symbol per text.

items.prompt: A bus station labels platforms in a Map. What does this program print?

options.feedback: Right. The number 7 and the text "7" are different keys, so the Map holds two entries and get(7) finds the first.
You treated both keys as the same text, as an object would. A Map keeps the type of every key, so 7 and "7" stay apart.
The size is right, but get(7) does not match "7". A Map compares keys exactly, with no type conversion.

items.explanation: A Map compares keys by value and type, so 7 and "7" are two keys. The size is 2, and get(7) returns the entry stored under the number.
hints: Compare the two keys on lines 2 and 3.
A Map does not convert keys to text the way an object does.
Count how many different keys were stored, then ask which one get asks for.

items.prompt: A library tracks loans in a Map keyed by member card objects. Which statement explains the second line printed?

options.text: Object keys are compared by reference, so a new object with equal contents is a different key.
options.feedback: Right. get finds an entry only for the very same object that was stored.

options.text: Object keys are compared by contents, so both lookups find the entry.
options.feedback: Then the last line would print 2 as well. A Map never looks inside a key object, only at whether it is the same object.

options.text: A Map turns object keys into text, so every object becomes the same key.
options.feedback: Then both lookups would give 2. A Map keeps the object itself as the key and does not convert it.

items.explanation: A Map compares object keys by identity. The literal on the last line is a new object, so no entry matches it, and get returns undefined.
hints: Look at what is passed to get on lines 3 and 4.
Two objects are equal only when they are the same object.
Ask whether line 4 passes the stored object or a fresh one.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: A fruit stall restocks plums, then lists the Map. Fill the blanks so it prints plum 6 and then fig 9.

options.feedback: Right. Setting an existing key replaces its value and keeps its place in the order.
A Map has no add method; calling it throws a TypeError. That method belongs to Set.
Right. Looping over a Map directly gives [key, value] pairs, which the brackets unpack.
This gives only the names, so each name is unpacked into letters and the program prints p l and f i.
Object.entries reads own properties, and a Map keeps its entries elsewhere, so the loop never runs.

items.explanation: set on an existing key updates it in place, so plum stays first. A for...of loop over the Map itself yields [key, value] pairs in insertion order.
hints: Line 3 changes an existing entry; line 4 chooses what to loop over.
Maps are iterable and produce [key, value] pairs.
Use the method that stores a value under a key, and loop over the Map itself.

items.prompt: The plant shop should print 8, the cactus price, but prints undefined. Tap the buggy line and pick the fix.

options.feedback: Right. set stores an entry that get can find later.
A Map has no add method, so this line throws a TypeError. The method for a Map takes a key and a value but has another name.
get only reads. It ignores the second argument and stores nothing, so the program still prints undefined.

items.explanation: Square brackets on a Map add an ordinary property to the object, not an entry. Entries are written with set and read with get.
hints: Compare line 3 with the way line 2 stores a value.
A Map keeps entries with its own methods, not with property syntax.
Use the same method as line 2, with the cactus name and price.

items.prompt: Write the body of countKinds(items). Use a Map to count each value and return the counts as an array of [value, count] pairs in first-seen order.
items.explanation: Read the current count with get, fall back to 0 for a new key, and write back one more with set. Spreading the Map gives its entries in insertion order. A Map keeps 1 and "1" apart.
hints: Keep one Map and update it inside a loop over items.
get returns undefined for a key that is not stored yet, so give it a starting number.
Store the old count plus one under the item, then spread the Map into an array.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: A hiking log records each viewpoint it passes. How many viewpoints does this program print?

options.feedback: Right. The second add of lake does nothing, so the Set holds lake, ridge and pass.
You counted every add call. A Set stores a value only once, so repeating lake does not grow it.
You removed both copies of lake. A Set keeps one copy of a repeated value; it does not remove it.

items.explanation: A Set keeps each value once. Adding "lake" a second time changes nothing, so the three different names give a size of 3.
hints: Look at which names appear more than once.
Adding a value that is already in a Set has no effect.
Count the different names, not the add calls.

items.prompt: A sensor sends NaN twice. Which statement explains the two lines this program prints?

options.text: A Set treats NaN as equal to itself, even though === does not.
options.feedback: Right. A Set uses its own sameness test, in which NaN matches NaN.

options.text: A Set compares values with ===, so both NaN entries are kept.
options.feedback: Then the size would be 3. A Set does not use ===; it counts NaN as one repeated value.

options.text: A Set keeps every value you give it, repeats included.
options.feedback: Then the size would equal the length of the list. A Set does not keep repeated values.

items.explanation: === says NaN is not equal to NaN, but a Set uses a sameness test where NaN equals NaN. The two NaN entries collapse into one, leaving NaN and 5.
hints: Compare the result of line 2 with the size on line 3.
A Set does not decide sameness with ===.
Ask how many different values remain if NaN matches NaN.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: A box office wants each ticket id once. Fill the blanks so the program prints [4, 9, 2] and then 3.

options.feedback: Right. The Set drops repeats, and spreading it gives back an array in first-seen order.
A Map expects pairs, and a plain number is not a pair, so this throws a TypeError before anything prints.
new Array(ids) wraps the whole list as one element, so nothing is removed and the spread array has a single entry.
Right. The spread result is an ordinary array, and an array reports its size with length.
size belongs to a Set or a Map. The spread result is an array, so size is undefined.

items.explanation: new Set(ids) keeps each id once, in the order first seen. Spreading it into square brackets builds a normal array, which reports its size through length.
hints: Line 2 builds an array from a collection.
Only one built-in collection removes repeated values.
The spread result is an array, not a Set. Which property does an array use to report how many entries it holds?
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: The party list should print 3, the number of VIP guests, but prints undefined. Tap the buggy line and pick the fix.

options.feedback: Right. A Set reports how many values it holds through size.
A Set has no count property, so this still prints undefined.
This wraps the whole Set in an array of one element, so it prints 1 whatever the Set holds.

items.explanation: A Set has no length. Its number of values is the size property. The second add of Ana is ignored, so the three different names give 3.
hints: Look at the property read on line 4.
Arrays use length; Sets use another name.
Read a property of vips itself, not of a wrapper around it. One of the two other names offered does not exist on a Set.

items.prompt: Write the body of shared(a, b). Return the values that appear in both arrays, each once, in the order of a. Use a Set.
items.explanation: Put b in a Set so has answers fast, then drop repeats from a with a second Set and keep the items found in the first. Spreading keeps the order of a.
hints: Build a Set from one array and loop over the other.
has tells you whether a value is in a Set, and add ignores repeats.
Spread a Set of a into an array, then filter it with has.

items.prompt: An office keeps notes in a WeakMap. What does this program print?

options.feedback: Right. An object key works, but a string is not allowed as a WeakMap key. The error ends the program before done.
You treated the WeakMap like a Map that takes any key. A WeakMap only accepts objects, so line 5 throws.
The entry for desk is still there, because desk is in use. A WeakMap does not drop entries right after they are set.

items.explanation: Line 3 stores a note under an object, and get returns it. A string is not an object, so line 5 throws a TypeError and done never prints.

A WeakMap needs objects as keys.
The first log works; look at what happens at line 5, and whether line 6 is reached.

items.prompt: A booking cache uses a WeakMap. Which statement explains why the last line prints undefined?

options.text: A WeakMap has no size property: it can only be asked about keys you already hold.
options.feedback: Right. A WeakMap cannot be counted or looped over, because its entries may disappear at any time.

options.text: size is undefined because the entry was already removed from the cache.
options.feedback: The line before prints true, so the entry is still there. size is undefined for another reason.

options.text: size is a method on a WeakMap, so it must be called as cache.size().
options.feedback: A WeakMap has no such method either. Calling it would throw a TypeError instead of printing.

items.explanation: A WeakMap does not expose its entries: no size, no keys, no loop. You can only call get, set, has and delete with a key you already hold.
hints: Compare the two lines printed.
A WeakMap hides its contents so that entries can be cleaned up.
Ask which operations a WeakMap offers without a key in hand.
items.author: claude-fable-5-2/unit-author

items.prompt: Order the lines so the attic is marked as visited, checked, and then a fresh empty object is checked. It should print true, then false.
items.explanation: The WeakSet and the object must exist before add runs. The check of room comes after add, so it prints true. A new empty object was never added, so its check prints false.
hints: Find the two lines that create values the others use.
add must run before the has check that should print true.
Each has check needs the value it asks about to exist, and the add must come before the check that prints true.

This stores the note under a brand new object. get(crate) looks up a different key, so it prints undefined.

items.prompt: Write the body of canBeKey(value). Return true when value can be used as a WeakMap key and false when setting it throws. Use try and catch.
items.explanation: Try to store the value in a fresh WeakMap. If set throws, the value cannot be a key, as with a string, a number or null. null looks like an object under typeof but is rejected.
hints: Let the WeakMap decide: try to use the value as a key.
set throws a TypeError for a value that cannot be a key, such as a string, a number or null.
Return true after a successful set inside try, and false inside catch.

items.prompt: A gym creates two lockers with the same label. What does this program print?

options.feedback: Right. Every Symbol call makes a new unique value, and a symbol prints with its description inside Symbol().
The label is only a description for people. Two symbols made by separate calls are never equal.
The comparison is right, but a symbol prints as Symbol(locker), not as its bare description.

items.explanation: Each call to Symbol returns a new, unique value, whatever the description. The description only appears when the symbol is shown, as Symbol(locker).
hints: Compare how the two symbols on lines 1 and 2 are created.
The text given to Symbol is a description, not an identity.
Two separate calls give two different values; check how console.log shows one.

items.prompt: A card object uses a Symbol key for its PIN. Which statement explains the two lines printed?

options.text: Object.keys skips Symbol keys, but the symbol still reads the value.
options.feedback: Right. Symbol keys are left out of the usual key listings, yet anyone who holds the symbol can read the property.

options.text: A Symbol key is private, so no code can read it, not even with the symbol.
options.feedback: The last line prints 4821, so it was read. Symbol keys are hidden from listings, but they are not locked.

options.text: Object.keys lists Symbol keys too, as the text pin.
options.feedback: Object.keys returns only string keys. The symbol never shows up there, and it would not appear as plain text.

items.explanation: Object.keys returns only string-named keys, so the symbol key is missing from the list. Reading card[secret] works for any code that has the symbol.
hints: Compare what line 4 lists with what line 5 reads.
Symbol keys are skipped by listing functions, not by property access.
The list lacks the symbol key, but the symbol itself still opens the property.

items.prompt: A bakery shares one symbol per product code. Fill the blanks so the program prints true and then sku.

options.feedback: Right. Symbol.for looks up a shared symbol in the global registry, or creates it, so equal text gives the same symbol.
Right. keyFor returns the registry text of a symbol that came from Symbol.for.
description is a property of a symbol, not a method of Symbol. Calling it throws a TypeError.
Symbol.iterator is a symbol value, not a function. Calling it throws a TypeError.

items.explanation: Symbol.for returns the same symbol for the same text, so a and b are equal. Symbol.keyFor gives back that registry text.
hints: Compare line 1 with line 2: what must make a and b the same symbol?
A registry returns the same symbol for the same text.
The first blank creates or finds a shared symbol; the second reads its text.

items.prompt: The greenhouse should print weekly, but prints undefined. Tap the buggy line and pick the fix.

options.feedback: Right. A property stored under a symbol is read with that symbol in square brackets.
This looks up the text water, which is a different key from the symbol, so it still prints undefined.
Symbol("water") makes a new symbol, which is not the stored one, so it prints undefined.

items.explanation: fern.water reads a string key named water, and no such key exists. The property lives under the symbol value, so it must be read with fern[water].
hints: Compare how line 2 stores the value with how line 3 reads it.
Dot syntax and quoted names always mean string keys.
Read it with square brackets around the variable that holds the symbol.

items.prompt: Write the body of countNotes(texts). Store each text in one object under its own new Symbol("note") key. Return how many symbol keys it holds, read with Object.getOwnPropertySymbols.
items.explanation: Every Symbol("note") call is a new key, so each text gets its own property, even equal texts. Object.keys ignores symbol keys, so the symbols are read with getOwnPropertySymbols.
hints: Create a fresh symbol inside the loop, once per text.
Separate Symbol calls give separate keys, so nothing is overwritten.
Assign box[Symbol("note")] in the loop and count the result of getOwnPropertySymbols.
